question: What is the main job of self-tolerance in our immune system?

options.A: To prevent the immune system from attacking healthy body tissue
options.B: To destroy foreign invaders like bacteria and viruses
options.C: To increase the production of red blood cells
options.D: To help white blood cells mature in the lymph nodes

explanation: Think of self-tolerance as the immune system's security check. It helps white blood cells recognize our own body parts so they don't mistakenly attack healthy organs!

question: What actually happens during an autoimmune response?

options.A: Red blood cells begin attacking invading bacteria
options.B: The immune system mistakenly attacks healthy body tissues
options.C: The body stops producing white blood cells completely
options.D: Foreign invaders rapidly multiply without any immune resistance

explanation: Autoimmunity happens when the immune system gets confused and treats our own healthy cells like dangerous enemies. You've got this!

question: What do we mean by 'molecular mimicry' in autoimmune conditions?

options.A: A pathogen shares protein structures with body tissue, confusing the immune system
options.B: Antibodies completely change their shape to match a virus
options.C: Immune cells hide inside healthy organs to escape detection
options.D: Healthy cells pretend to be foreign invaders to trick white blood cells

explanation: Sometimes a germ looks very similar to our own body tissue. When the immune system fights the germ, it accidentally attacks the body tissue too because they look like twins!

question: Why does a failure in cell death (apoptosis) lead to autoimmune disease?

options.A: Bone marrow stops making new white blood cells
options.B: Pathogens are allowed to hide inside dying cells
options.C: Healthy cells die too quickly and release too many nutrients
options.D: Autoreactive lymphocytes survive instead of undergoing programmed cell death

explanation: Normally, rogue immune cells that could attack our body are told to self-destruct. When that fails, these harmful cells stick around and cause trouble.

question: What part do environmental factors play in kicking off an autoimmune disease?

options.A: They directly replace damaged genes in the bone marrow
options.B: They cure chronic inflammation by boosting white blood cells
options.C: They prevent the formation of autoantibodies
options.D: They can act as triggers that awaken an underlying immune vulnerability

explanation: Think of genetics as the loaded gun, and environmental triggers—like a nasty infection or stress—as the finger pulling the trigger.

question: A patient asks why they got an autoimmune disease while their sibling living in the same house did not. What best explains this?

options.A: Viral infections only affect the oldest sibling in a family
options.B: Differences in genetic susceptibility and individual environmental triggers
options.C: Autoimmune diseases are entirely contagious between household members
options.D: The sibling must have a stronger immune system due to diet

explanation: Even in the same house, no two people have the exact same genes or identical life exposures, which changes everyone's unique disease risk.

question: What is the big difference between organ-specific and systemic autoimmune diseases?

options.A: Systemic conditions are caused exclusively by viral infections
options.B: Systemic diseases only affect the skin, while organ-specific affect the brain
options.C: Organ-specific conditions cannot be treated with medication
options.D: Organ-specific targets a single tissue, while systemic affects multiple organs

explanation: Organ-specific focuses its attack on just one place (like the thyroid), while systemic conditions cause widespread chaos across many parts of the body.

question: Which of these is a well-known systemic autoimmune disease?
explanation: Lupus (SLE) is classic for being systemic—it can affect the skin, joints, kidneys, and heart all at once!

question: What does an Antinuclear Antibody (ANA) blood test look for?

options.A: The amount of oxygen bound to hemoglobin
options.B: The total number of red blood cells in circulation
options.C: The presence of bacterial pathogens in the bloodstream
options.D: The presence of antibodies that attack the body's own cell nuclei

explanation: An ANA test checks for rogue antibodies that target the control center (nucleus) of our cells, which helps doctors spot systemic autoimmune issues.

question: Why is getting an autoimmune disease diagnosed often a long and tricky journey?

options.A: Blood tests are completely unavailable for most autoimmune conditions
options.B: Early symptoms are vague, overlapping, and resemble many other common illnesses
options.C: Autoimmune markers change completely every single day
options.D: Patients rarely report their symptoms to healthcare providers early on

explanation: Early signs like tiredness and body aches look like everyday malaria or stress, making it tough for doctors to pin down right away.

question: A patient having an autoimmune flare has extreme fatigue and stiff joints. What is a great initial nursing action?

options.A: Restrict all fluid intake to prevent swelling in the joints
options.B: Help the patient plan daily activities and schedule mandatory rest periods
options.C: Advise the patient to stop taking all prescribed medications immediately
options.D: Encourage the patient to push through the fatigue with rigorous exercise

explanation: Energy conservation and pacing are wonderful nursing interventions. We help clients save their strength for what matters most without burning out.

question: Why do nurses need to monitor organ function regularly in patients with systemic autoimmune conditions?

options.A: It prevents patients from developing contagious bacterial infections
options.B: It eliminates the need for any future blood tests
options.C: Widespread inflammation can silently damage vital organs like the kidneys and heart
options.D: It proves whether the patient is following their prescribed diet

explanation: Systemic flare-ups don't just hurt joints—they can quietly cause internal damage over time, making routine checkups a lifesaver.

question: What is the main goal of medications used to treat autoimmune diseases?

options.A: To permanently eliminate all white blood cells from the body
options.B: To suppress the hyperactive immune response and reduce inflammation
options.C: To cure the genetic mutation that caused the disease
options.D: To replace lost body fluids during an acute infection

explanation: These drugs act like a calm-down pill for an overactive immune system, stopping it from attacking healthy tissues.

question: What major risk must nurses watch out for when patients take long-term immunosuppressant drugs?

options.B: Increased susceptibility to severe opportunistic infections
options.C: Total loss of taste and smell
options.D: Excessively high blood pressure caused by thickened blood

explanation: When we quiet the immune system to stop it from attacking the body, it also struggles to fight off normal germs. Good patient education on hygiene is key here!

question: What is a major long-term risk for patients dealing with ongoing autoimmune inflammation and immunosuppression?

options.A: Increased risk of cardiovascular disease and infections
options.B: Complete regeneration of destroyed organ tissue
options.C: Permanent stabilization of normal blood pressure
options.D: Total immunity against all forms of cancer

explanation: Constant inflammation wears down blood vessels over time, and medicines that lower immunity leave patients more open to infections.

question: Why is mental health and psychological support so important for patients with long-term autoimmune conditions?

options.A: Patients with autoimmune diseases lose their memory over time
options.B: Mental stress is proven to be the sole biological cause of all autoimmune flares
options.C: Psychological counseling replaces the need for anti-inflammatory medications
options.D: Coping with chronic, unpredictable physical illness often leads to anxiety and depression

explanation: Living with unpredictable pain and tiredness is mentally exhausting. Caring for the whole patient means supporting their mind as well as their body!
